title: How Fish Survive −1.9°C Water Without Freezing 🧊
description:
Why don't Antarctic fish freeze solid in seawater colder than their blood's normal freezing point? Icefish and their cousins make antifreeze proteins that bind to tiny ice crystals and stop them growing, and the gene for them evolved from a digestive enzyme gene.

topic: Why don't Antarctic fish freeze solid?
script: Your goldfish would freeze solid in this minus 1.9 degree water, so how does this fish survive? The sea around Antarctica stays liquid because salt lowers its freezing point. But normal fish blood freezes at about minus 0.7. So a regular fish would turn into a fishsicle. The trick is hiding in its blood. Antarctic icefish and their cousins make antifreeze proteins. When a tiny ice crystal sneaks inside, the proteins grab onto its surface and stop it from growing. The crystal stays too small to do harm. Scientists even found ice in their spleens, all year round. And the wildest part? The antifreeze gene evolved from a gene for a digestive enzyme. Evolution recycled a gut gene into a winter coat. So would you trade your blood for antifreeze and swim in minus 1.9 degree water?
key_facts: Seawater around Antarctica sits near -1.9 C, kept liquid by salt
Typical marine fish blood freezes at about -0.7 C
Notothenioid fish (icefish and relatives) make antifreeze glycoproteins that bind to ice crystal surfaces and stop growth
Ice crystals have been found in their spleens year-round (Cziko et al. 2014, PNAS)
The antifreeze glycoprotein gene evolved from a trypsinogen (digestive enzyme) gene (Chen, DeVries, Cheng 1997, PNAS)
